item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

The first hours after a serious cyber incident are filled with activity. Security starts investigating, IT works to contain the impact, legal begins assessing potential obligations, and executives want to know what happened and what the company is doing about it. Most teams rely on the same tools they use every day to coordinate that work, which usually means email, Slack, Teams, shared documents and video calls.

Coordination gets much more complicated when the company’s email or collaboration environment is part of the incident. Email may still work, employees may still be able to join meetings, and nothing on the surface may suggest that the organization has lost control of its communications. Meanwhile, an attacker with access to accounts used by responders may read the team’s messages, monitor containment plans or impersonate someone involved in the response.

Something shifted in offensive security over the last eighteen months that most organizations haven’t fully absorbed yet. It isn’t that attackers got smarter. It’s that the economics of attack changed entirely — and those of us who run red teams have had a front-row seat to the transformation.

The conversation about AI in cybersecurity tends to fixate on defense: better anomaly detection, faster triage, and AI-assisted SOC analysts. That framing misses the more urgent story. item.title: 🟠 The AI trust deficit: Why explainability, not more automation, is the CIO’s next priority
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

An AI trust deficit occurs when an organization deploys autonomous AI agents faster than it can prove those agents are acting within policy. It’s the gap between what AI agents are doing and what CIOs can clearly explain to a board, auditor, or regulator. Closing that gap requires audit-ready context: evidence showing who owns an agent, what it can access, and which policies governed its decisions.

This gap is widening quickly. More than half of enterprises are already deploying agentic AI, according to Omdia research, and these agents now onboard applications, resolve access requests, and act on business data around the clock. The question is no longer whether AI can move fast. It’s whether you can prove, at any moment, that it moved correctly.

Why the AI trust deficit is a board-level problem

item.title: 🔵 Governing the agent workforce: New data on the next frontier of AI risk
item.description:
Why this matters: Compliance/regulatory signal — determine applicability and required action.

In the fast-paced world of agentic AI, building agents and defending ROI is yesterday’s news. Today, the more pressing challenge is managing and governing the exploding workforce of agents to mitigate growing enterprise risk.

The problem intensifies as AI agents move from advisory to more active roles. According to a survey of 200 IT and AI decision makers conducted by Foundry and Rubrik, most agents are allowed to act with full (26%) or limited (35%) autonomy.

With access to enterprise systems and authority to execute end-to-end tasks, governance, guardrails, and compliance have become key obstacles to AI agent implementation. This was cited by 42% of survey respondents, along with AI agent management, at 18%. Almost one quarter of respondents (24%) cited security and governance as the biggest barrier to their ability to scale agents, even over technical complexities (17%) and lack of proven ROI (14%).

item.title: 🔴 The moat is dry – Part 1: Why the old security model failed
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

In June 2017, a piece of malware called NotPetya got into Merck & Co. without climbing a single wall. It arrived through a backdoor in accounting software supplied by a Ukrainian vendor, the kind of trusted, routine traffic every perimeter is built to let through. It spread to some 40,000 of the drugmaker’s computers, and Merck put the damage at more than $1.4 billion.

Then several of Merck’s insurers argued they owed nothing, because the attack was attributed to Russian military intelligence and their policies excluded acts of war. The fight ended in a confidential settlement in January 2024.

Two lessons sit in that story. The moat didn’t matter, because the threat came in with the traffic the moat was designed to admit. And the people who price risk for a living were the first to notice and the first…

Black-box models that process data mysteriously and generate unverified outputs are no longer acceptable under frameworks like the EU AI Act. Organizations must be prepared to audit the entire lifecycle of their models.

The core issue for compliance officers is verification. When an AI pipeline assists in determining creditworthiness, analyzing patient diagnostics, or managing civic resource distribution, the underlying software must be auditable from end to end. item.title: 🟠 Your AI agent learned a better way. Who approved the change?
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Imagine a support team working through complaints after a service outage. Its refund policy normally requires an eligibility review. For this incident, an authorized manager approves an exception: customers on the verified outage list may receive up to $100 without individual review, through Friday.

An agent processes those cases successfully. Later, the system consolidates those case histories into a reusable memory: small, immediate refunds resolve service complaints quickly. The summary preserves the outcome but loses the outage restriction and expiration date.

The following week, the agent retrieves that guidance for a similar complaint from a customer who was not affected by the outage. It issues a refund without review. The payment service checks the agent’s credentials and the dollar limit, but does not check whether the customer qualifies for an active exception.

No attacker is needed in this hypothetical. The case may close faster, yet the agent has begun applying a temporary exception beyond its authorized scope.
